focus_area_title: Recognize employees for speaking up by implementing a "Good Catch" program
content_text_body:
Recognizing employees for their suggestions to improve patient safety or for their reporting of "close callsâ€ or "near missesâ€ will increase the likelihood that these "speaking up behaviorsâ€ will continue.  According to the 2004 book, "Patient Safety: Achieving a new standard for care,â€ good catches can occur up to 100 times more frequently than serious events but often go unreported in healthcare organizations!

### Why is it important?

One of the key actions to strengthen safety culture is to "recognize care team members who report adverse events and close calls, who identify unsafe conditions, or who have good suggestions for safety improvements.â€ This is according to the Joint Commission's 2017 article, "The essential role of leadership in developing a safety culture.â€ 

#### Make a Habit of Recognizing the Little Things

Recognizing employees for speaking up about patient safety will become more of a habit for you and your team if you develop a culture of recognition and positivity within your group. Start daily huddles or briefings by sharing 3 positive examples of patient care, teamwork, or kindness. You can also make it a goal to recognize three different team members a day for good performance.   

#### Share Safety Learnings or Suggestions with the Broader Team

According to research by James Reason, one of the leading figures in Patient Safety research, when leaders recognize and share "good catchesâ€ - in which adverse events are avoided - these valuable lessons become learning opportunities for employees among the broader team and the individual who "spoke upâ€ is positively reinforced for doing so (i.e., feedback loop is closed).  

#### Implement a "Good Catchâ€ or "Safety Heroesâ€ program within your team or organization.  

**Some examples are below:**

- Memorial Hermann Health System calls it a "good catchâ€ when a report causes clinicians to identify a potentially harmful action and intervene prior to causing harm. Good catches occur about 1,000 times a month in the system's hospitals. 

- Medical University of South Carolina Health (MUSC Health) issues a daily email highlighting a near-miss, error or unsafe condition and each month recognizes "safety starsâ€ - employees who have made these reports. If care team members want closure in the reporting structure, they can ask to be personally notified with a result at the conclusion of the review.

- Mazur and coauthors found that a good catch program in the Department of Radiation Oncology at the University of North Carolina had a positive impact on the organization's quality and safety efforts, resulting in improvements in the patient safety culture and in patient satisfaction. After investigating 560 good catches, they discovered more than half of the good catches occurred in situations caused by performance issues such as not following standardized processes and poor communication.

- The Children's Hospital of Penn State Health Milton S. Hershey Medical Center found its good catches increased by 240% after establishing a "Great Catch" program in the Pediatric Acute Care Unit. In the published study, employees found that reporting good catches resulted in immediate action from nursing leadership and led to increased reporting of good catches in other units within the hospital.

- A patient care assistant in a Pennsylvania hospital was transferring a patient into a bed with locked wheels when the bed moved, despite the wheels being locked. Although the patient was not harmed, the patient care assistant raised the issue during one of her unit's daily safety huddles, which led to examining all of the beds on the unit. Facility personnel discovered that the wheel locks on 60% of the beds on the unit needed repair, which led to hospital-wide wheel-lock inspection and repair. The patient care assistant was recognized by the Pennsylvania Patient Safety Authority in the 2017 "I Am Patient Safety" campaign
